course: Young Animal Milk Replacer and Supplement Feeding

lessons.title: Understanding Milk Replacer Ingredients: Sources and Functions
lessons.body: Milk replacers are formulated to mimic the composition of maternal milk for young animals. The main ingredients fall into categories: protein sources, fat sources, carbohydrates, vitamins, minerals, and additives. Protein sources include skim milk powder, whey protein concentrate, casein, soy protein isolate, and egg protein. Skim milk powder is highly digestible but expensive; whey protein is cheaper and contains lactose. Soy protein is plant-based and cost-effective but contains anti-nutritional factors unless processed. Fat sources include animal fats (tallow, lard), vegetable oils (coconut, palm, soybean), and specialty fats like MCT oil. Carbohydrates are mainly lactose from whey or skim milk; some products use maltodextrin or glucose. Vitamins and minerals are added as premixes. According to FAO, local milk powder suppliers in Africa often blend skim milk powder with vegetable fats to reduce cost. For example, in Kenya, a common piglet milk replacer contains 24% protein, 10% fat, and 0.5% fibre, costing about KES 500 per kg. In Nigeria, calf milk replacer with 20% protein and 15% fat sells for NGN 3,500 per 10 kg bag. Teagasc (Ireland) recommends that milk replacers for calves should have at least 20% protein and 15% fat, with lactose between 40-50%. Denkavit, a Dutch company, produces milk replacers with specific protein sources like whey and casein for different species. For goat kids and lambs, milk replacers often use skim milk powder and animal fat, with 22-24% protein and 20-25% fat. Puppies and kittens require higher protein and fat: Royal Canin puppy milk replacer has 33% protein and 40% fat, while kitten milk replacer has 40% protein and 25% fat. MaxCare (NZ) produces colostrum supplements and milk replacers for calves, lambs, and kids, emphasising the use of spray-dried bovine colostrum. University extension services, such as those from Iowa State University, provide tables of nutrient requirements for young animals. When selecting ingredients, consider digestibility, cost, and availability. Common mistakes in Africa include using human milk powder (which lacks sufficient protein and fat for animals), mixing replacers with too little water (causing diarrhoea), and storing powder in humid conditions leading to caking. Always check the label for guaranteed analysis and expiry date. For piglets, a milk replacer with 28% protein, 20% fat, and 0.5% fibre is ideal; feed at 37°C, 200 ml per litre of water, and offer 0.5-1 litre per day per piglet. For calves, mix 125 g powder per litre of water at 40°C, feed 10-12% of body weight daily. For goat kids, 150 g per litre at 39°C, feed 15% of body weight. For lambs, 200 g per litre at 39°C, feed 10-15% of body weight. For puppies, 1 part powder to 2 parts water at 38°C, feed 15-20% of body weight. For kittens, 1 part powder to 3 parts water at 38°C, feed 20-25% of body weight. These figures are based on NAP (National Academies Press) nutrient requirements and manufacturer guidelines. Local suppliers in Africa, such as Unga Farm Care in Kenya and Vital Feed in Nigeria, offer milk replacers, but quality varies. Always buy from reputable sources and follow mixing instructions precisely.

lessons.title: Protein Sources in Milk Replacers: Dairy vs Plant Proteins
lessons.body: Protein is the most critical nutrient in milk replacers for young animals, as it supports rapid growth and immune function. Dairy proteins are superior to plant proteins for young animals because they are highly digestible and contain essential amino acids. Skim milk powder (SMP) contains about 34% protein, mainly casein and whey. Whey protein concentrate (WPC) has 35-80% protein, depending on processing. Casein is the primary protein in milk, forming curds in the stomach for slow digestion. For calves, Teagasc recommends that milk replacers contain at least 20% protein, with 75% of it from dairy sources. Denkavit uses a blend of whey and casein to achieve a protein efficiency ratio similar to maternal milk. Plant proteins, such as soy protein isolate (SPI) and soy flour, are cheaper but contain anti-nutritional factors like trypsin inhibitors and oligosaccharides that cause digestive upset. However, properly processed soy protein (e.g., soy protein concentrate) can replace up to 50% of dairy protein in calf milk replacers without affecting performance, according to University of Illinois extension. For piglets, soy protein is less tolerated; NAP recommends that piglet milk replacers use only dairy proteins for the first two weeks. In Africa, local milk powder suppliers often blend SMP with vegetable proteins to reduce cost. For example, in Kenya, a piglet milk replacer with 24% protein may contain 50% SMP and 50% soy protein concentrate, costing KES 450 per kg. In Nigeria, calf milk replacer with 20% protein may use 70% SMP and 30% soy flour, selling for NGN 3,000 per 10 kg. Common mistakes include using raw soy flour, which causes diarrhoea, and over-relying on plant proteins, leading to poor growth. For goat kids and lambs, dairy proteins are preferred; MaxCare (NZ) uses spray-dried bovine colostrum and skim milk powder. Puppies and kittens require high-quality animal proteins; Royal Canin uses poultry and fish proteins in their milk replacers. When mixing, use a protein source that is easily digestible. For calves, mix 125 g powder per litre of water at 40°C, providing 25 g protein per litre. For piglets, mix 200 g per litre at 37°C, providing 48 g protein per litre. For goat kids, 150 g per litre at 39°C, providing 33 g protein per litre. For lambs, 200 g per litre at 39°C, providing 44 g protein per litre. For puppies, 1 part powder to 2 parts water at 38°C, providing 33% protein on dry matter. For kittens, 1 part powder to 3 parts water at 38°C, providing 40% protein on dry matter. These ratios are based on NAP and manufacturer guidelines. In Africa, cost is a major factor: dairy proteins are expensive, so farmers may use plant proteins, but this can lead to poor growth and increased mortality. Always check the protein source on the label. FAO recommends that milk replacers for young animals should have a protein digestibility of at least 90%. If using local milk powder, ensure it is fresh and stored properly. Common mistakes include mixing with hot water (above 50°C) which denatures proteins, and using chlorinated water which kills beneficial bacteria. Always follow the manufacturer's instructions for mixing and feeding.

lessons.title: Fat and Energy Sources: Ensuring Adequate Calories
lessons.body: Fat is the primary energy source in milk replacers, providing essential fatty acids and aiding in the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. Young animals have high energy requirements: calves need about 20% fat in milk replacer, piglets 20%, goat kids 25%, lambs 30%, puppies 40%, and kittens 25%. Fat sources include animal fats (tallow, lard, butterfat) and vegetable oils (coconut, palm, soybean, sunflower). Coconut oil is rich in medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs), which are easily digested and provide quick energy. Palm oil is cheap but high in saturated fat; soybean oil is high in polyunsaturated fat. According to Teagasc, calf milk replacers should contain 15-20% fat, with a blend of animal and vegetable fats for optimal digestibility. Denkavit uses a proprietary fat blend that mimics milk fat composition. MaxCare (NZ) uses tallow and coconut oil in their lamb and kid milk replacers. In Africa, local milk powder suppliers often use palm oil or tallow to reduce cost. For example, in Kenya, a calf milk replacer with 15% fat may use 80% tallow and 20% coconut oil, costing KES 400 per kg. In Nigeria, piglet milk replacer with 20% fat may use 100% palm oil, selling for NGN 2,800 per 10 kg. Common mistakes include using rancid fats (which cause diarrhoea) and not emulsifying fats properly (leading to separation). Fats must be homogenised into the powder. When mixing, use warm water (40-45°C) to dissolve fat. For calves, mix 125 g powder per litre at 40°C, providing 19 g fat per litre. For piglets, 200 g per litre at 37°C, providing 40 g fat per litre. For goat kids, 150 g per litre at 39°C, providing 38 g fat per litre. For lambs, 200 g per litre at 39°C, providing 60 g fat per litre. For puppies, 1 part powder to 2 parts water at 38°C, providing 40% fat on dry matter. For kittens, 1 part powder to 3 parts water at 38°C, providing 25% fat on dry matter. These figures are based on NAP and Royal Canin guidelines. Energy density is crucial: piglets need 4.5 kcal/ml, calves 4.0 kcal/ml, goat kids 4.8 kcal/ml, lambs 5.0 kcal/ml, puppies 5.5 kcal/ml, kittens 5.0 kcal/ml. If energy is too low, animals lose weight; if too high, they get diarrhoea. In Africa, many farmers use full-fat soy flour as a fat source, but it contains anti-nutritional factors. Instead, use vegetable oil blends. FAO recommends that milk replacers for young animals should have a fat digestibility of at least 85%. Always store fat-containing powders in a cool, dry place to prevent rancidity. Common mistakes include mixing with cold water (fat solidifies) and using excessive fat (causing scours). Follow the manufacturer's mixing instructions precisely.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates, Vitamins, and Minerals: The Supporting Cast
lessons.body: Carbohydrates in milk replacers are primarily lactose, which is easily digested by young animals due to high lactase activity. Lactose content should be 40-50% for calves, 45-55% for piglets, 40-50% for goat kids and lambs, and 30-40% for puppies and kittens. Some milk replacers use maltodextrin or glucose as partial replacements, but lactose is preferred. According to NAP, lactose intolerance can occur if too much is fed, leading to diarrhoea. In Africa, local milk powder suppliers may use sucrose or starch, which are poorly digested by young animals. For example, in Kenya, a cheap piglet milk replacer may contain 30% lactose and 20% sucrose, costing KES 350 per kg, but this causes scours. In Nigeria, calf milk replacer with 40% lactose and 10% maltodextrin sells for NGN 2,500 per 10 kg. Vitamins and minerals are added as premixes to meet requirements. Key vitamins: A, D, E, K, B-complex, C. Key minerals: calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, potassium, sodium, chloride, iron, copper, zinc, manganese, selenium, iodine. Teagasc recommends that calf milk replacers contain 0.8% calcium and 0.6% phosphorus. Denkavit includes chelated minerals for better absorption. MaxCare (NZ) adds selenium and vitamin E for immune support. Royal Canin includes taurine for kittens and puppies. In Africa, many milk replacers lack adequate vitamins and minerals, leading to deficiency diseases. For example, in Kenya, a goat kid milk replacer without added copper caused swayback in kids. In Nigeria, a lamb milk replacer without selenium caused white muscle disease. Common mistakes include using table salt (sodium chloride) instead of a balanced mineral mix, and exposing vitamins to heat (which destroys them). When mixing, use water at 40°C to preserve vitamins. For calves, mix 125 g powder per litre at 40°C, providing 0.5 g calcium per litre. For piglets, 200 g per litre at 37°C, providing 0.8 g calcium per litre. For goat kids, 150 g per litre at 39°C, providing 0.9 g calcium per litre. For lambs, 200 g per litre at 39°C, providing 1.0 g calcium per litre. For puppies, 1 part powder to 2 parts water at 38°C, providing 1.0% calcium on dry matter. For kittens, 1 part powder to 3 parts water at 38°C, providing 1.2% calcium on dry matter. These figures are based on NAP and manufacturer guidelines. In Africa, cost is a barrier: a complete vitamin-mineral premix costs about KES 1,000 per kg, so some farmers omit it. This leads to poor growth and disease. FAO recommends that milk replacers should contain a balanced vitamin-mineral premix. Always check the label for guaranteed analysis. Common mistakes include mixing with hard water (high minerals) and storing powder in sunlight (destroys vitamins). Follow the manufacturer's instructions and use clean equipment.

lessons.title: Practical Formulation and Cost Management in Africa
lessons.body: Formulating milk replacers in Africa requires balancing nutritional needs with local ingredient availability and cost. The goal is to match the nutrient profile of maternal milk as closely as possible. Start with a base of skim milk powder or whey powder, then add fat, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals. For calves, a typical formula: 50% skim milk powder, 20% whey powder, 20% tallow, 5% coconut oil, 3% vitamin-mineral premix, 2% emulsifier. This yields 22% protein, 18% fat, 45% lactose. Cost: in Kenya, skim milk powder KES 600/kg, whey KES 400/kg, tallow KES 200/kg, coconut oil KES 300/kg, premix KES 1,000/kg. Total cost per kg: (0.5*600)+(0.2*400)+(0.2*200)+(0.05*300)+(0.03*1000)+(0.02*500)=300+80+40+15+30+10=KES 475/kg. In Nigeria, similar formula costs NGN 3,500/kg. For piglets, use 60% skim milk powder, 15% whey, 20% fat blend, 3% premix, 2% emulsifier. Cost: KES 550/kg. For goat kids, 50% skim milk powder, 20% whey, 25% fat blend, 3% premix, 2% emulsifier. Cost: KES 500/kg. For lambs, 40% skim milk powder, 25% whey, 30% fat blend, 3% premix, 2% emulsifier. Cost: KES 520/kg. For puppies, 40% skim milk powder, 20% whey, 30% fat blend, 5% premix, 5% emulsifier. Cost: KES 600/kg. For kittens, 50% skim milk powder, 15% whey, 25% fat blend, 5% premix, 5% emulsifier. Cost: KES 620/kg. These costs are estimates; actual prices vary. Local suppliers in Africa: Kenya - Unga Farm Care, Pembe Flour Mills; Nigeria - Vital Feed, Grand Cereals; South Africa - Meadow Feeds, Epol. Imported brands: Denkavit, MaxCare, Royal Canin. Common mistakes: using human milk powder (e.g., Nido, Cow & Gate) which has wrong nutrient profile; mixing with too much water (dilution); using dirty water (bacterial contamination); not weighing powder (using spoons leads to inconsistency). Always use a digital scale. Mixing instructions: for calves, 125 g powder per litre of water at 40°C, feed 10-12% of body weight daily. For piglets, 200 g per litre at 37°C, feed 0.5-1 litre per day. For goat kids, 150 g per litre at 39°C, feed 15% of body weight. For lambs, 200 g per litre at 39°C, feed 10-15% of body weight. For puppies, 1 part powder to 2 parts water at 38°C, feed 15-20% of body weight. For kittens, 1 part powder to 3 parts water at 38°C, feed 20-25% of body weight. Feeding frequency: calves 2-3 times daily; piglets 4-6 times; goat kids 3-4 times; lambs 3-4 times; puppies 4-6 times; kittens 4-6 times. Always feed at body temperature (37-39°C). Store powder in airtight container in cool, dry place. Use within 4 weeks of opening. In Africa, humidity causes caking; add silica gel packets. Cost management: buy ingredients in bulk, share with neighbours, use local substitutes like fresh cow milk (but adjust for fat and protein). FAO recommends that farmers be trained in least-cost formulation. Teagasc offers online calculators. Denkavit provides technical support. MaxCare has mobile apps. Royal Canin has veterinary diets. University extension services (e.g., University of Nairobi, Ahmadu Bello University) offer courses. Common mistakes: overfeeding (causes diarrhoea), underfeeding (starvation), sudden diet changes (stress). Always transition gradually. Monitor weight gain weekly. If diarrhoea occurs, reduce volume and consult a vet. With proper formulation and management, young animals can thrive on milk replacers, reducing mortality and improving growth.

quiz.q: Which protein source is most commonly used in calf milk replacers because of its high digestibility?
quiz.explanation: Skim milk powder is highly digestible and provides excellent amino acid balance for young calves.

quiz.q: What is the typical crude protein content of a high-quality calf milk replacer?
quiz.explanation: Calf milk replacers usually contain 20 to 28 percent crude protein to meet growth needs.

quiz.q: Which fat source is often added to milk replacers to increase energy density?
quiz.explanation: Tallow is a common animal fat used to raise the energy content of milk replacers.

quiz.q: At what temperature should milk replacer be fed to young calves to avoid digestive upset?
quiz.explanation: Milk replacer should be fed at approximately body temperature, 37 to 39 degrees C, for proper digestion.

quiz.q: Which ingredient in milk replacer can cause digestive problems if it replaces too much milk protein?
quiz.explanation: Soy protein isolate is less digestible for very young calves and can cause scours if overused.

quiz.q: What is the main function of lecithin in milk replacer powder?
quiz.explanation: Lecithin helps mix fat evenly into the powder and keeps it suspended when mixed with water.

quiz.q: A farmer mixes 150 g of milk replacer powder in 1 L of water. What is the approximate dry matter percentage?
quiz.explanation: 150 g in 1 L water gives about 15 percent dry matter, which is a common mixing rate.

quiz.q: Which vitamin is often added to milk replacers to prevent white muscle disease in calves?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin E and selenium are added to prevent white muscle disease.

quiz.q: What is the best water temperature for mixing milk replacer powder?
quiz.explanation: Mixing at 40 to 50 degrees C helps dissolve powder without destroying nutrients.

quiz.q: Which mineral is important in milk replacer to support bone growth and is often balanced with phosphorus?
quiz.explanation: Calcium and phosphorus are critical for bone development in young animals.

quiz.q: What does the term milk replacer mean?
options: A) A substitute for whole milk
B) A solid feed for calves
quiz.explanation: Milk replacer is a powder mixed with water to replace or supplement whole milk.

quiz.q: Which ingredient is a common carbohydrate source in milk replacers?
quiz.explanation: Lactose from milk sources is the main carbohydrate in quality milk replacers.

quiz.q: Why is fiber content kept low in milk replacers for young calves?
options: B) Calves cannot digest fiber well before rumen development
C) Fiber makes milk too sweet
quiz.explanation: Young calves have an undeveloped rumen and cannot efficiently digest high fiber ingredients.

quiz.q: Which of these is a plant protein sometimes used in milk replacers but needs careful processing?
quiz.explanation: Soy protein concentrate is used but must be processed to improve digestibility for calves.

quiz.q: What is the recommended feeding rate of milk replacer powder per calf per day in the first week?
quiz.explanation: Calves typically receive 150 to 250 g of powder daily in the first week, split into feedings.

quiz.q: Which additive is used in milk replacers to prevent scours caused by bacteria?
quiz.explanation: Antibiotics are sometimes added to control bacterial scours, though use is regulated.

quiz.q: What happens if milk replacer is mixed too thin?
options: A) Animal gets too much energy
B) Animal may lose weight and be hungry
quiz.explanation: Thin mixing reduces nutrient intake, leading to hunger and poor growth.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a common ingredient in milk replacers?
quiz.explanation: Grass hay is a solid feed and not used in liquid milk replacer formulas.

quiz.q: What is the role of emulsifiers in milk replacer?
options: B) Keep fat mixed with water
quiz.explanation: Emulsifiers help fat blend evenly with water so the animal gets consistent energy.

quiz.q: Which milk protein is most allergenic to young calves when used in large amounts?
quiz.explanation: Soy protein can cause allergic reactions and digestive upset in very young calves.

quiz.q: A calf weighs 40 kg and needs 10 percent of body weight in milk replacer solution daily. How many liters is that?
quiz.explanation: 10 percent of 40 kg is 4 kg, which is about 4 L of milk replacer solution.

quiz.q: Which storage condition is best for milk replacer powder?
quiz.explanation: Cool, dry storage prevents caking, mold, and nutrient loss.

quiz.q: What is the main energy source in milk replacer?
quiz.explanation: Fat provides the most energy in milk replacers for young animals.

quiz.q: Which vitamin is important for vision and immune function in calves and is often added to milk replacer?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin A supports vision, growth, and immunity in young animals.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of poor quality milk replacer?
options: A) Fine powder that mixes easily
quiz.explanation: Clumping and poor mixing often indicate old or low-quality powder.

quiz.q: Which ingredient provides lactose in milk replacer?
quiz.explanation: Whey powder is rich in lactose, a key energy source for young animals.

quiz.q: Why should milk replacer not be fed at temperatures above 45 degrees C?
options: B) It can scald the animal and destroy nutrients
quiz.explanation: Very hot liquid can burn the mouth and esophagus and damage heat-sensitive nutrients.

quiz.q: Which of these is a mineral commonly added to milk replacers for iron supplementation?
quiz.explanation: Ferrous sulfate is an iron source used to prevent anemia in young animals.

quiz.q: What is the approximate fat content of a standard calf milk replacer?
quiz.explanation: Most calf milk replacers contain 10 to 20 percent fat for energy.

quiz.q: Which practice helps prevent digestive problems when changing milk replacer brands?
options: B) Mix old and new gradually over several days
C) Stop feeding for a day
quiz.explanation: Gradual transition helps the digestive system adjust and reduces scours risk.
